sections.h2: What does the Maricopa County Recorder do?
sections.html:
The Maricopa County Recorder's Office keeps the public record of documents that affect land in the county, and it also runs voter registration and mail voting. The office reports more than 52 million recorded documents and voter registration for more than 2.6 million eligible voters. For a home seller the relevant work is recording the deed that moves title and the deed of trust that releases or replaces the old loan.

The office cannot give legal advice, will not help complete documents, and does not provide notary services. If you are unsure which form to record, a title company, estate planner or attorney has to answer that. The recording phone line is 602-506-3535.

Maricopa County is the largest county in Arizona. It covers 9,224 square miles, had 4,420,568 residents in the 2020 census, and contains fifteen cities and ten towns, from Phoenix (the county seat) to Gila Bend and Wickenburg. Recording happens at one downtown office no matter where in that area the house sits.

sections.h2: Where and how can you record a deed in Maricopa County?
sections.html:
You can record in person, by mail or electronically. The document has to be an original or a government-issued certified copy. The downtown office is at 301 W Jefferson St, Suite 200, Phoenix, AZ 85003, open Monday through Friday from 8:00 a.m. to 5:00 p.m., excluding holidays, with no appointment needed. An in-person original comes back to you right away.

  • In person: cash, card or check are accepted. Check payee is Maricopa County Recorder.
  • By mail: send to Attn. Copy Desk at the same address with a check, cashier's check or money order. The recorded original is mailed back to the return address in 2 to 4 weeks, and the office does not promise same-day recording of mailed documents.
  • Electronic: digital recording accounts are built for high-volume customers. A single document can go through a third-party submitter instead.

Most sellers never visit. The title or escrow company at closing records the deed for you, so the practical task is making sure the deed and its affidavit are signed correctly before closing day.

sections.h2: How much does it cost to record a document in Maricopa County?
sections.html:
The standard fee is $30 per document, regardless of length, under A.R.S. 11-475. The Recorder's published fee page lists the rest.

ItemFee
Most documents (not plats or surveys)$30
Government agency recording, most documents$15
Plats and surveys, first page$24
Plats and surveys, each added page$20
Copy of a recorded document, per page$1
Certification, per document$3
Military discharge documents$0
Child support documents$0

Source: Maricopa County Recorder fee schedule.

The office collects fees up front, so a mailed deed should arrive with the right total. Ask your title company which separate charges, if any, appear on your settlement statement.

sections.h2: What must a Maricopa County deed include to be recorded?
sections.html:
A deed needs either an Affidavit of Property Value or an exemption code. The Recorder's FAQ says the affidavit records the selling price, date of sale and other details about the sale, and a deed that fits an exemption can carry the code on its face instead. The office cannot say which code fits your deed.

The statute behind this is A.R.S. 11-1133. A deed that transfers title, and any contract of sale, must have an affidavit signed by seller and buyer or their agents, on a form approved by the Department of Revenue. It asks for these items:

  • Names, mailing addresses and phone numbers of buyer and seller
  • The name and address for the tax statement
  • The complete legal description, the situs address and the assessor's parcel number
  • The date of sale and total consideration, including cash down payment and the type of financing
  • Whether personal property received is 5% or more of the price
  • The relationship of the parties, and for a house, whether it will be owner-occupied or rented

The recorder must refuse a deed that lacks a complete affidavit unless it carries an exemption notation. Form rules for the document itself, such as a caption and margins, come from A.R.S. 11-480 and the office's form requirements page.

sections.h2: How does recording connect to property tax in Maricopa County?
sections.html:
The deed you record is how the Assessor learns who the new owner is and where to send the tax statement, which is why the affidavit asks for a tax-statement address. The Treasurer then bills that owner. If a house sells in the fall, find out whether the first half has been paid. In Maricopa County it is due October 1 and delinquent after 5:00 p.m. on November 1 (November 2 in 2026, since the first fell on a Sunday), and the full-year deadline is December 31.

Property tax is a lien, and A.R.S. 42-17153 says it attaches on January 1 of the tax year and ranks ahead of other liens except state liens and tax liens from other years. A title company will therefore expect any unpaid tax to be settled from your proceeds at closing. The Maricopa County Treasurer takes questions on amounts due at 602-506-8511.

The Assessor's site also links to Maricopa Title Alert, a free document registration notification service provided through the Recorder's Office. Owners who inherited a house or live out of state can use it to keep an eye on their title. The Treasurer collects for more than 1,800 tax districts, including cities, schools, community colleges and special districts, so one bill covers many levies. The Treasurer's site also lists excess proceeds from foreclosure sales that brought in more than the amount owed, under A.R.S. 33-812.

sections.h2: What should a seller check before recording day?
sections.html:
A short checklist prevents most rejected recordings.

  • Names on the deed match the names on the title exactly, including any trust.
  • The legal description and parcel number match the prior deed.
  • The Affidavit of Property Value is signed, or an exemption code is written on the deed.
  • The document is an original, signed, and any notary block is complete.
  • The return address is typed on the upper left of the first page.
  • The fee total is correct for the number of documents, at $30 each.

Where a house passes through a probate or trust, the deed chain can be longer than usual, and each document recorded carries its own fee. Ask the title company for a list of what will be recorded and a total.

faqs.q: How much does the Maricopa County Recorder charge to record a deed?
faqs.a: It charges $30 per document for most documents, regardless of page count, under A.R.S. 11-475. Plats and surveys cost $24 for the first page and $20 for each added page. Copies are $1 per page and certification is $3 per document.

faqs.q: Where is the Maricopa County Recorder's office?
faqs.a: The downtown office is at 301 W Jefferson St, Suite 200, Phoenix, AZ 85003. It is open Monday through Friday, 8:00 a.m. to 5:00 p.m., excluding holidays, and no appointment is needed to record in person.

faqs.q: Can I mail a deed to the Maricopa County Recorder?
faqs.a: Yes. Mail the original, with the right fee by check, cashier's check or money order, to Attn. Copy Desk at 301 W Jefferson St, Suite 200, Phoenix, AZ 85003. The recorded document is mailed back in 2 to 4 weeks, and the office does not guarantee recording on the day it receives a mailed document.

faqs.q: Does a deed need an Affidavit of Property Value in Maricopa County?
faqs.a: Yes, unless it carries an exemption code. A.R.S. 11-1133 requires the affidavit on a deed that transfers title, and the recorder must refuse a deed without a complete affidavit or an exemption notation. The Recorder's office cannot advise which exemption applies.

faqs.q: Will the Maricopa County Recorder help me fill out a deed?
faqs.a: No. The office cannot provide legal advice or help complete documents, and it does not offer notary services. Use a title company, estate planner or attorney. For recording questions, call 602-506-3535.
